variants.name: Future.add_done_callback with a bound callback token
variants.implementation_notes: The token in Python is the asyncio object that will be completed: a Future (or Task) is handed to the service side, the client attaches its completion action with Future.add_done_callback - a bound callback such as functools.partial(handler, request) - and the event loop invokes exactly that callback when the operation settles, so completions are demultiplexed by registration instead of by scanning a table of outstanding requests. The library nature of this realization is the point: asyncio owns the storage and the dispatch, while the per-request state sits in the callback's arguments. Where the program can simply await, the coroutine frame carries the state and no explicit token is needed; implicit per-request state travels in contextvars.
variants.code_sketch:
fut = loop.create_future()
pending[req.id] = fut
fut.add_done_callback(functools.partial(handle, req))   # callback = the token
transport.send(req)                                     # service completes it later
# from another thread: loop.call_soon_threadsafe(fut.set_result, reply)
pitfalls: asyncio.Future is explicitly documented as not thread-safe: complete it or attach callbacks from another thread only through loop.call_soon_threadsafe.
set_result/set_exception raise InvalidStateError when the future is already done or cancelled - the documented guard is to check first, and a task can be cancelled by its creator at any time.

Callbacks on an already-done future are scheduled with call_soon, never run inline, and the loop keeps only weak references to tasks: a fire-and-forget task can be collected mid-flight and its exception never retrieved unless a strong reference is kept.
contextvars must be created at module level (never inside a closure, because a Context holds strong references); a Token can be reset only once and re-entering an entered Context raises RuntimeError.

variants.name: Ready-queue dispatch with loop.call_soon
variants.implementation_notes: The queued-completion strategy: instead of attaching a callback to a token object, the completing side posts the whole operation - handler plus bound arguments - onto the loop's ready queue, and the loop dispatches it in order. Suits completions arriving from other threads or foreign event loops, code where no future exists yet, and cases where strict FIFO order of completions matters; the cost is that the pending state lives in the closure arguments rather than in an inspectable future, and the returned asyncio.Handle is the only handle on the request.
variants.code_sketch:
handle = loop.call_soon_threadsafe(functools.partial(on_reply, req, dispatch))
# ... later, if the request is abandoned:
handle.cancel()          # the asyncio.Handle is the cancellable token for that completion
pitfalls: A cancelled Handle silently drops the completion: nothing records the abandonment, so pair cancellation with the registry that owns the request state.
call_soon keeps strong references to its arguments until dispatch, so long-pending entries pin whatever the partial closes over.
